title: How the Maori Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Maori, the Polynesian people who settled New Zealand (Aotearoa). They cover the migration from a legendary homeland called Hawaiki, traditional structured warfare with clubs (kaika and patu), the musket wars after firearms arrived around 1807-1815, the 1835 French annexation rumor that led to the Treaty of Waitangi, the New Zealand Wars, cultural loss and revival from the 1970s, official language status for Te Reo Maori in 1987, and the Maori cultural concepts of mana and whakapapa. They also discuss moko face tattoos (carved with chisels), the haka dance and All Blacks, and modern Maori population and social statistics. The episode ends with listener mail about doll hairs currency and an outro.

segments.title: Opening banter and pronunciation
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on the Maori, discuss pronunciation, the movie Once Were Warriors, and the common perception of Maori face tattoos.

segments.title: Maori migration and name
segments.summary: The Maori are generally accepted in academic circles as the first settlers of New Zealand, arriving from Polynesia between about 1280 and 1450, possibly from a mythical homeland called Hawaiki, which scholars think combines real islands like Tahiti, Samoa and the Cook Islands. They named the land Aotearoa, meaning land of the long white cloud. The name Maori means ordinary or common, in contrast to Europeans called pakeha.

segments.title: Traditional warfare, weapons and mana
segments.summary: Maori tribal warfare was structured and often held after the harvest, fought with short clubs (kaika) and cutting-edge clubs (patu), with relatively few deaths compared to later firearms. Wars were often over mana, prestige, and control of land.

segments.title: Musket Wars
segments.summary: Europeans brought firearms and Maori traded goods such as pigs, flax and potatoes, and also women, for muskets. Around 1807 a tribe first used muskets in battle, struggled with them, and then began the Musket Wars around 1815, which were bloody until everyone had guns and the fighting leveled off. About twenty Maori and New Zealanders died in the early phase, per the hosts' summary.

segments.title: Chatham Islands, French annexation rumor and Treaty of Waitangi
segments.summary: Two tribes displaced by musket wars moved south and attacked the Moriori on the Chatham Islands, enslaving and killing them. In 1835 a rumor that France would annex New Zealand led Maori to ally with the British and sign the Treaty of Waitangi, which they later felt the British violated over land and taxes, leading to the New Zealand Wars.

segments.title: Anglicization, language loss and revival
segments.summary: After the wars the Maori population was in danger; missionaries created a written Maori alphabet. Urbanization after World War Two and government suppression of Maori culture weakened it. A 1970s awakening led to Maori Language Week in 1975, the first bilingual school in 1998, and Te Reo Maori becoming one of New Zealand's three official languages in 1987 (the hosts said ninety five; this was stated in the episode). Land claims through the Waitangi Tribunal continued.

segments.title: Whakapapa, mana types and spoken word
segments.summary: Maori culture is spiritual, with belief in ancestors and supernatural beings. Whakapapa, genealogy, is central and is often shared only with trusted people. Mana comes in forms: inherited by birth, granted by others for good deeds, and of the group, plus karero (spoken word), and oral historians were trained to memorize history.

segments.title: Haka, moko tattoos and modern statistics
segments.summary: The haka is a dance performed before battle, and the All Blacks perform it before rugby games. Moko are chiseled tattoos, with kiri tuhi as a less sacred form. Maori population has grown to about 4 million in New Zealand, with about 14 percent Maori, and the hosts cite social problems including alcoholism and crime rates.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener mail from Talent Wisdom about paying his girlfriend in doll hairs and buying Zimbabwe dollars on eBay. The hosts close with ways to contact the show.
